text.p: Swedish media group Tidnings AB Marieberg said on Tuesday that its daily newspaper division would show a worse result in 1996 than 1995.
"1996 will not at all be at the level of 1995," managing director Bengt Braun told a breakfast meeting.

Media operations, including overseas newspapers and new media products, made an operating profit of 113 million crowns in the first nine months of 1996 compared to a profit of 252 million crowns in the same period year earlier.
Braun pointed out that changes to daily paper Dagens Nyheter during 1996 had been received well by readers.
An evaluation of its weekend edition is completed and Marieberg will not continue with it.
But the company will start a free newspaper.

Braun said the free paper would be handed out in the underground railway stations similarly to free newspaper Metro that was set up in Stockholm over a year ago by media group Kinnevik with great success.
Braun said the company's growth overseas is good, especially in Poland and there was potential for further growth in Scandinavia and Eastern Europe.
"The advertising market (in Eastern Europe) is growing quicker than the economy at large," he said.
Marieberg can expand overseas by increasing its ownership in existing companies or through new companies, he said.
"We will do more things in the countries we are in now. Our overseas interests will grow," he said.
Braun said he saw no reason to change Mareberg's recent move into commercial television, acquiring a stake of channel TV4.
He said Marieberg would not reduce its stake in TV4 or any other business despite criticism by the Swedish authorities.
Braun said Marieberg's hold of the media sector would be reduced over time as more actors came into the market.
Marieberg has currently no plans to increase its stake further in TV4. The company is still interested, however, in its own TV project in the future.
Braun did not want to forecast the development in the advertising market but pointed out that this is linked to a large degree to private consumption and to Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
At an analysts' meeting in November last year Braun said the business area New Media was expected to show a loss of between 35-40 million crowns for 1996.
"We have no new information to give," he said on Tuesday.
